title: Indian ancestry among jazz musicians and Indian music
summary: Blanton was young and part Indian; Dance and Edison ask whether an Indian element survives in jazz.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, I was just going to say, when you had Blanton he wasn't as developed as he was --
Oh, no, he was nothing but a kid. He'd just come from Tennessee. He's from Nashville.
This was what made me mention it earlier on. There must be some Indian thing in this music.
Though you possibly can't sort of dissect it, pull it out, but there must -- just as sort of African things have survived, so must the Indian thing. I mean, they had music, didn't they.

Sure, they did. But it was just a thing that the blacks added to it that you can't describe, but you hear the Indians play now, their native music, and hear Art Tatum play or Louis Armstrong play, there's quite a difference in the feeling. Quite a difference in the feeling because the blacks, we have something going that makes you happy, everybody happy. It will make an Indian happy, it will make an African happy, it will make a European happy, it will make an Arab happy, it will make a Jewish person happy.
Indian music doesn't get to all those people like the jazz does.
It doesn't reach you like -- when you go all over the world, jazz -- everybody knows jazz. You can hear a jazz record, I don't care where you go. Louie Armstrong has made that possible.
